title: TransPlace: Transferable Circuit Global Placement via Graph Neural Network

problem.claim: Global placement optimizes the physical layout of computer chips to improve chip performance.

gap.claim: Existing global placement methods optimize each circuit independently from scratch and neglect transferable knowledge, limiting efficiency and chip performance as circuit complexity increases.

contributions.claim: TransPlace provides global placement by learning continuous-space layouts for millions of cells with varying sizes.
The framework uses Netlist Graph modeling, Cell-flow and relative position encoding, and a tailored graph neural network architecture to represent and parameterize placement knowledge.
The framework applies a two-stage coarse-to-fine placement strategy.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Compared with state-of-the-art placement methods, TransPlace reportedly places unseen circuits with a 1.2x speedup while reducing congestion by 30%, timing by 9%, and wirelength by 5%.

narrative_sequence.summary: Global placement is important for optimizing computer-chip performance.
Prior methods optimize circuits independently and do not exploit transferable knowledge.
TransPlace learns placement for millions of mixed-size cells using graph representations, invariant encoding, a graph neural network, and coarse-to-fine placement.
The authors report speed and placement-quality improvements on unseen circuits relative to state-of-the-art methods.

source_observation.claim: The framework learns placement knowledge across circuit designs and applies it to unseen circuits.

interpretation.claim: Learning transferable representations may reduce repeated optimization effort when related instances share structural information.

application.claim: For repeated optimization over structurally related designs, consider representations and models that separate reusable knowledge from instance-specific placement decisions.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish when transfer fails or whether the reported gains generalize beyond the evaluated unseen circuits.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the training and evaluation circuit sets, dataset size, or experimental protocol.
The abstract does not define the reported timing metric or provide statistical variation and ablation results.
The abstract does not describe computational resource requirements or implementation details.
